Mind the Gap

EXPLORING WAYS TO PRESENT GAPS & GAP TRENDS

Achievement Gaps

• IMHO, the most abused and misunderstood of
academic indicators.

• With the advent of criterion-referenced testing, gaps
in percent pro cient have become ubiquitous.

• Used as part of almost all state accountability
systems.

• Not only gaps themselves but trends in gap statistics.

Mountains & Mole Hills

• My motivation for thinking about this came from the recent initiative led by Morgan
Polikoff to move away from pro ciency based cuts, especially for looking at gaps.

• Experts proposed looking at scale score differences.

• http://www.npr.org/sections/ed/2016/07/18/486196906/here-s-an-idea-ask-experts-
how-to-rate-schools

• This is analogous to issue of whether to use percent above cut or mean for SGPs.

• This is an issue regarding how to describe the difference in central tendency of two
distributions (gaps). It’s mostly a minor technical issue.

• A less technical interest relates to how to communicate gaps to be meaningful.

• After rst declining this approach by states, feds seem to be amenable to it.
Massachusetts included it in their ESSA application.

Scratch a Criterion and you find norm

• It’s not clear (to me) that scale score based gap/gap-trend indicators are (much
of) an improvement.

• One loses the important pro ciency cut as a reference point in the gap.

• Though pro ciency cuts are designed to make the scale interpretable. Even
with pro ciency based cuts, it’s not clear that differences in percent pro cient
are that interpretable.

• Is a 20% gap between economically and non-economically disadvantaged
students the same: 0%/20%, 40%/60%, and 80%/100%.

• This takes me back to the same deliberations I went through when thinking
about student growth and writing Norm- and criterion-referenced student growth.

Norm- and Criterion-Referenced Gap Metrics

• Goal: Produce a metric-free distributional comparison for looking at gaps.

• Goal: Communicate a 50th percentile student who is white lies at what percentile
of the overall distribution.

• Extend: Communicate an Xth percentile student who is of ethnicity Y lies at what
percentile of the overall distribution.

• Extend: Do this for other groups (e.g., (non)-economically disadvantaged)

• Question: Would it be better to depict where an overall Xth percentile student
like in each of the ethnicity speci c distributions? Problem (bigger numbers are
worse).

• Gaps a achievement level cuts can be depicted by locating cut graphically.

Distribution-Free Gap Metrics

• Bene t: Gaps are more interpretable. If 50th percentile is used for
gap, then one is looking at the difference in percentage of students
below “grade level”.

• Bene t: Gaps can defensibly be compared in different grades. E.g., Are
achievement gaps larger in Grade 4 Math or Grade 8 Math?

• Bene t: Gaps can defensibly be compared in different content areas.
E.g., Are achievement gaps larger in Grade 7 ELA or Grade 7 Math?

• Bene t: Gaps can defensibly compared in different states using
different tests. E.g., Are achievement gaps in Grade 4 ELA larger in
Colorado than Georgia

Questions/Observations

• The differences between approaches aren’t dramatic.

• Comparison of gaps across grades using percent
pro cient are questionable based upon where the
cut is placed (Andrew Ho). This would also apply to
cross state comparisons.

• Comparison of gaps across grades using scale scores
requires some though. Cross state comparisons
wouldn’t be possible.

Next Steps

• This seems like a useful analysis/representation that any state could run to better
understand gaps.

• The current graphical representation suffers from the disadvantaged group being
above the advantaged group. Probably needs to be reversed but not sure how.

• Create an R package (e.g., CenterforAssessment_Tools) that contains data tools a
state could use on its data based upon an assumed format provided.

• Staff with analyses/diagnostics that states could run on their data are welcome to
contribute and build out the package.

• The package could be used with our work with states or used by a test vendor in
conjunction with their data validation.
